(CNN)  -- Los Alamos National Laboratory announced Wednesday it is notifying nearly 2,000 current and former employees and visitors that they may have been exposed to beryllium in the lab and may be at risk of disease. Officials are trying to determine the source of beryllium found at Los Alamos National Laboratory. "Letters went out to all of them today," said Kevin Roark, a spokesman for the New Mexico laboratory. Concern over possible exposure to the hard, gray metal, which is purified for use in nuclear weapons and reactors and also used in bicycle frames and golf clubs,  was first raised last November, when a box containing beryllium was received at the laboratory's short-term storage facility, he said. "The package appeared to have damage or degradation of the packing materials, which prompted us to test the area for additional contamination," he said. Surface contamination was found, but it turned out that the box was not the source, Roark said, adding that the source has not been determined. Since the contaminated area had not been tested for the presence of beryllium since 2001, everyone who has entered the restricted-access area since then is being alerted, he said. "It's just one building at one technical area," Roark said, noting that the laboratory covers 36 square miles and has nearly 10,000 employees. Beryllium is hazardous only when its fine, particulate form is inhaled, he said. It was found on surfaces, not in the air, he said.  Find out more about beryllium » . Roark said the alert was sent because "we think it's the responsible, prudent thing to do to let people know we discovered this contamination and to answer their questions if they have any concern about potential for exposure." There are no reports of sickness and "we don't expect anyone to be ill," he said. The laboratory said about 240 employees and 1,650 visitors were potentially at risk because they visited the contaminated areas. About 2 percent of the exposed employees could become sensitized, a smaller percentage of whom could develop chronic beryllium disease, Roark said. Inhalation of powdered beryllium can result in chronic beryllium disease, which can impair lung function in people who are susceptible. The risk to the visitors would be "extremely low" because of the activities they performed and their short exposure time, Roark said. An operator will be available at the laboratory at 505-665-7233 from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mountain Time, Monday through Friday.

# Los Alamos National Laboratory Alerts Nearly 2,000 to Potential Beryllium Exposure

Los Alamos National Laboratory has begun notifying approximately 2,000 current and former employees, along with visitors to the facility, that they may have been exposed to beryllium during their time at the site and could face an associated risk of disease. The notification effort represents a significant undertaking by lab officials to ensure that anyone who may have encountered the toxic metal is properly informed and can seek appropriate medical monitoring.

## Origins of the Investigation

The concern surrounding potential beryllium exposure first came to light in November, when a damaged box containing the material arrived at the laboratory's short-term storage facility. The visible damage to the container prompted safety officials to conduct testing in the surrounding area, a precautionary measure that ultimately revealed surface contamination within the facility.

## An Unresolved Source

Despite subsequent investigation, the exact source of the beryllium contamination remains undetermined. Notably, laboratory officials were able to rule out the damaged box itself as the origin of the contamination, meaning the true source of how beryllium came to be present on surfaces in the area is still unknown. This uncertainty has added complexity to the investigation, as officials work to understand how and when the contamination may have occurred.

## Scope of the Notification

The scale of the notification effort stems from a critical gap in testing history: the contaminated area had not been checked for beryllium presence since 2001. Given this extended timeframe, laboratory officials made the decision to alert every individual who had entered the restricted-access area at any point since that year. This precautionary approach has resulted in a notification list encompassing roughly 240 employees and an additional 1,650 visitors who accessed the facility during this period.

## Assessing the Actual Risk

While the notification effort is extensive, officials have emphasized several important details that help contextualize the level of concern. The contamination that was discovered existed solely on surfaces within the facility—testing did not detect any beryllium presence in the air. This distinction is significant because beryllium poses a genuine health hazard primarily when it exists in a fine particulate form that can be inhaled into the lungs. Surface contamination alone, without airborne particulates, presents a considerably lower risk profile.

Furthermore, officials have confirmed that there are currently no reports of illness connected to this exposure incident. This absence of reported health effects, combined with the surface-only nature of the contamination, suggests that while notification and monitoring remain prudent precautionary measures, the immediate health risk to those being contacted may be limited. Nonetheless, the laboratory continues to prioritize transparency and thoroughness in reaching out to all potentially affected individuals, allowing them to make informed decisions about any follow-up medical screening they may wish to pursue.

# Beryllium Exposure at Los Alamos: A Legacy of Risk Comes to Light

For decades, workers at Los Alamos National Laboratory handled beryllium—a lightweight metal prized for its unique properties in nuclear weapons components—often without fully understanding the health risks lurking in its dust and fumes. Today, the laboratory continues to grapple with the consequences of that historical exposure, even as it implements modern safety protocols to protect current employees.

## A Metal Essential to the Mission

Beryllium has been used at Los Alamos since the earliest days of the Manhattan Project. Its properties—including its ability to reflect neutrons—made it valuable in nuclear weapons design and production. However, beryllium dust and particulates, when inhaled, can trigger a severe immune response in sensitized individuals, leading to Chronic Beryllium Disease (CBD), an incurable and sometimes fatal lung condition.

Unlike acute chemical exposures with immediate symptoms, beryllium sensitization can remain latent for years or even decades before manifesting as illness, complicating both detection and historical accountability.

## How the Problem Came to Light

Awareness of beryllium's dangers grew gradually within the nuclear weapons complex. Occupational health researchers and industrial hygienists began identifying patterns of lung disease among beryllium workers at various Department of Energy (DOE) facilities starting in the mid-20th century, though understanding of the disease's mechanisms improved significantly in later decades.

At Los Alamos specifically, retrospective medical surveillance and monitoring programs—implemented as scientific understanding of beryllium sensitization improved—helped identify affected workers, including some who had left the laboratory years earlier. Compensation claims filed under federal programs, including the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act (EEOICPA) established in 2000, brought renewed attention to the scope of historical exposures, as former workers and their families sought recognition and support for beryllium-related illnesses.

## Current Response and Safety Measures

In response to this legacy, Los Alamos and the DOE have implemented several measures:

- **Medical surveillance programs** that monitor current and former workers for beryllium sensitization through blood tests (the Beryllium Lymphocyte Proliferation Test)
- **Engineering controls** including improved ventilation systems and containment procedures in areas where beryllium is machined or handled
- **Personal protective equipment** requirements for workers in beryllium-associated tasks
- **Site characterization efforts** to identify legacy contamination in older facilities
- **Compensation assistance** helping affected workers navigate federal programs designed to provide benefits for occupational illness

The laboratory has also worked to establish clearer exposure limits, often adopting standards more stringent than historical OSHA permissible exposure limits as scientific understanding of beryllium sensitization at low doses has evolved.

## Ongoing Challenges

Despite these measures, challenges remain. Legacy contamination in aging infrastructure can be difficult and costly to remediate. Former workers, particularly those who worked at the lab decades ago, may struggle to document exposure history for compensation claims. And the latent nature of beryllium disease means new cases may continue to emerge among individuals exposed years or decades in the past.

Worker advocacy groups have periodically pressed for more aggressive medical monitoring, clearer accountability for historical practices, and streamlined compensation processes for affected individuals and families.

---

*Note: This piece provides a general framework based on publicly known patterns regarding beryllium exposure at DOE nuclear facilities. For a piece intended for publication, specific dates, named officials, exact statistics on affected workers, and direct quotes would need to be verified through primary sources such as DOE reports, Los Alamos National Laboratory communications, EEOICPA claims data, and interviews with affected workers, medical professionals, and lab officials.*

**RIVERSIDE COUNTY** — Health officials confirmed yesterday that an estimated 47 employees at the Hartwell Nuclear Research Facility may have been exposed to airborne beryllium particles following a ventilation system failure in the facility's metallurgy testing wing.

## Incident Overview

The exposure occurred during routine machining operations on beryllium-containing components used in neutron reflector research. According to facility spokesperson Diane Kowalski, an air filtration malfunction went undetected for approximately six hours before monitoring equipment triggered containment protocols.

"We take any potential exposure extremely seriously," Kowalski said. "The affected wing was immediately sealed, and all personnel underwent decontamination procedures per federal guidelines."

## Health Risks

Beryllium exposure poses significant health concerns, according to Dr. Elena Martinez, an occupational health specialist consulted for this story. Inhalation of beryllium dust or fumes can cause:

- **Acute beryllium disease** — a chemical pneumonitis causing inflammation of lung tissue
- **Chronic beryllium disease (CBD)** — a progressive granulomatous lung condition that can develop years after exposure, even from relatively low-level contact
- **Beryllium sensitization** — an immune response that may precede CBD in genetically susceptible individuals
- Skin irritation and contact dermatitis from direct exposure

Dr. Martinez emphasized that not everyone exposed to beryllium develops disease, but symptoms of CBD—including persistent cough, fatigue, chest pain, and weight loss—can take months or years to manifest, making long-term medical monitoring essential.

## Facility and Agency Response

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission have both opened investigations into the incident. Hartwell facility management stated that:

- All potentially exposed workers have been offered immediate medical screening
- Blood beryllium lymphocyte proliferation tests (BeLPT) are being administered to assess sensitization
- The affected wing remains closed pending full inspection and filtration system repairs
- An independent industrial hygiene firm has been contracted to conduct air quality testing

The facility says it will provide ongoing medical monitoring for affected employees for a minimum of 20 years, consistent with federal beryllium exposure guidelines.

Report safety concerns: osha.gov/report

Environmental Health Division

1-800-CDC-INFO
Beryllium exposure information: cdc.gov/niosh/topics/beryllium

Affected workers seeking legal or medical guidance may also consult the **Beryllium Health Registry**, a voluntary monitoring program tracking long-term outcomes for exposed individuals.
